changes.before: CyberSentinel demonstrates how to evaluate a URL gateway as a connected system: measure the information its features supply, the corrections its expert can make and the cost of execution. The experiments reveal a benchmark-format dependency, derive an exact routing constraint and verify a client-path improvement. These findings guide representation, expert and service design.
changes.after: CyberSentinel shows how to judge a URL gateway as a connected system: by the signals behind its predictions, the corrections its expert can make and the time spent serving each request. Its experiments uncover a URL-format convention in the benchmark, derive an exact limit on routing between unchanged decisions and verify a 79.68% reduction in median paired p95 latency in the single-host synthetic structural-only service. Together, these findings turn measured model and service behavior into specific decisions about representation, expert selection and implementation.

changes.location: 5.1 Direct Answers to the Research Questions
changes.before: RQ1—Representation and transfer. Structural features add 64.07 percentage points of internal recall over length alone, with a 95% domain-clustered interval [59.99, 67.63], at false-positive rate (FPR) 0.7747%. Validation labels also follow a format convention whose share of the gain is unquantified. External certified FPR is 90.5487%, versus 9.4513% for length-only; the cascade adds no recall or expert calls (Tables 4.2–4.3). This finding motivates checking the signals behind a feature gain and measuring specificity on the intended source.
changes.after: RQ1—Representation and transfer. Structural features add 64.07 percentage points of internal recall over length alone, with a 95% domain-clustered interval [59.99, 67.63], at false-positive rate (FPR) 0.7747%. Validation labels also follow a URL-format convention, although the experiments do not quantify how much of the gain comes from that association. On external certified negatives, FPR is 90.5487%, versus 9.4513% for length-only, while the cascade adds no recall or expert calls (Tables 4.2–4.3). A feature gain is therefore most informative when its underlying signals and specificity are also tested on the intended source.

changes.before: The interventions make that test concrete. Scheme spelling changes frozen-model decisions. A separate refit removes scheme sensitivity while reducing true and false positives; its combined fitting and calibration changes require their own labeled evaluation. Paired outputs establish which errors an expert can correct. Shared errors survive every selection between those unchanged decisions.
changes.after: The controlled interventions show how to make that assessment. Changing scheme spelling changes frozen-model decisions, while a separate refit removes scheme sensitivity and reduces both true and false positives. Because the refit changes fitting and calibration together, its detection behavior requires its own labeled evaluation. Comparing both models on the same inputs then reveals which errors the expert can correct: if both misclassify a URL, choosing between their existing decisions leaves that error in place.

changes.location: 5.1 Direct Answers to the Research Questions
changes.before: RQ2—Monitoring and action. The GMM recognizes 115/132 external windows (87.12%), exceeding its 80% target. Its audit alerts are 28/252 windows (11.11%) against 5%, so sensitivity and false alerts must be assessed together. Ordered, stateful replay sends 8,253/8,701 requests (94.8512%) to the expert. The policy retains 69/69 gold detections and adds 218 certified false positives (Table 4.5). Recognizing a change in inputs does not tell a gateway which response will help. Following alerts into paired decisions supplies that test.
changes.after: RQ2—Monitoring and action. The GMM recognizes 115/132 external windows (87.12%), exceeding its 80% target, with 28/252 audit alerts (11.11%) against a 5% limit. Sensitivity and false alerts together describe the monitor's behavior; paired decisions show what its response contributes. Ordered, stateful replay sends 8,253/8,701 requests (94.8512%) to the expert, retaining 69/69 gold detections and adding 218 certified false positives (Table 4.5). This comparison gives monitoring a concrete design test: follow an alert through the routing decision and check whether the selected expert improves the outcome.

changes.location: 5.1 Direct Answers to the Research Questions
changes.before: RQ3—Inline tradeoffs. The fixed cascade meets the invocation and primary request-error limits. Pooled p95 is 364.30 ms against a 200 ms budget, and external false-alert safeguards are exceeded. The original 69-pair recall sample gives a corrected lower bound of −6.1533 percentage points under independent labeled-pair assumptions. That bound leaves the −2-point noninferiority margin unresolved; it does not establish inferiority (Tables 4.6–4.7 and 4.14). Measuring these quantities separately reveals where to intervene: detector computation and request handling need distinct experiments, alongside detection quality.

changes.location: 5.1 Direct Answers to the Research Questions
changes.before: Worker-owned clients improve the synthetic structural-only service; separate scoring tests quantify transformer cost. These experiments connect a proposed change to a measurable consequence. Representation stability is tested with labeled detection, expert selection with corrections, and monitoring with the decisions its alerts change.
changes.after: The client comparison turns that distinction into an improvement: worker-owned clients speed up the synthetic structural-only service, while separate scoring tests quantify transformer cost. Across these experiments, the same principle guides evaluation: assess representation stability together with labeled detection, select experts by the errors they correct, and judge monitoring by the decisions its alerts change.

changes.before: The benchmark investigation gives URL researchers a concrete check. All 20,209 validation negatives use HTTPS, versus 46.6362% of positives; the negative HTTPS indicator reaches AUC 0.7668. The fixed-weight external intervention also changes decisions. These findings justify checking format conventions before interpreting a gain as transferable detection, without quantifying the HTTPS-attributable fraction. Paired errors establish available expert corrections (Sections 4.8.1 and 4.10.2).
changes.after: The benchmark investigation gives URL researchers a simple check to add to evaluation: inspect whether formatting conventions track class labels. All 20,209 validation negatives use HTTPS, versus 46.6362% of positives, and the negative HTTPS indicator reaches AUC 0.7668. The fixed-weight external intervention also changes decisions, supporting a check of format dependence before interpreting a gain as transferable detection. These tests do not quantify the HTTPS-attributable fraction of the gain. Paired error analysis then identifies the corrections available from an expert (Sections 4.8.1 and 4.10.2).

changes.before: Table 4.21 tests spelling changes with weights fixed. Tables 4.16–4.17 verify exact scheme invariance after refitting and quantify detection changes. Different cohorts and fitting procedures prevent attributing the refit's effect to normalization alone. Together, the internal association and external intervention support a practical benchmark check; collection-source causality remains unresolved.
changes.after: The two interventions answer complementary questions: Table 4.21 tests spelling changes with weights fixed, whereas Tables 4.16–4.17 verify exact scheme invariance after refitting and measure the accompanying detection changes. Because the cohorts and fitting procedures differ, the refit's effect cannot be attributed to normalization alone. The internal association and external intervention therefore support a practical benchmark check while leaving the role of collection source as a separate causal question.

changes.before: Routing provides an exact design constraint: 2,261 shared false positives among 2,497 certified negatives impose a 90.5487% floor on unchanged-decision selection. Escalation adds 218 false positives without another gold detection. On the separate cohort, one expert repair is available, but wider gates select none and add 18 false positives. Count available corrections before tuning a gate. Service tests identify a client-path improvement with matching comparable predictions despite changed admission order (Tables 4.18–4.19). Table 4.23 measures expert cost separately.

changes.before: The recall-only analysis supports noninferiority conditional on independent labeled pairs. Every model detects every positive while flagging most negatives; the original gate calls no expert, and the wider gate adds false positives. Specificity and selected corrections therefore determine the practical value of the preserved recall. Reused observations provide neither independent replication nor guaranteed campaign independence.
changes.after: The recall-only analysis supports noninferiority conditional on independent labeled pairs. Every model detects every positive while flagging most negatives; the original gate calls no expert, and the wider gate adds false positives. The practical value of that preserved recall therefore depends on specificity and the corrections actually selected. Because the comparisons reuse observations, they do not provide independent replications or guarantee independence across campaigns.

changes.location: 5.2.2 Validity and Reuse of the Evidence
changes.before: The shuffled-label investigation explains a puzzling control result. Small residual coefficients can rank format-associated labels well despite nearly constant probabilities. Input audits check the fitted data, term removal measures one contribution, randomization reproduces the spread, and stricter optimization preserves it. Inspecting coefficients and score ordering alongside mean probability provides a practical test of such controls.
changes.after: The shuffled-label investigation shows how small residual coefficients rank format-associated labels despite nearly constant probabilities. Input audits check the data, term removal measures one contribution, and randomization and stricter optimization confirm persistent ranking variation. Coefficients, score ordering and mean probability together make these controls interpretable.
